1:
Job breaks his long silence under Zophar's last assault, and the witnesses read the opening of the reply as the ground-plan of the whole chapter. The reformed John Gill sets the target squarely: against Zophar's assertion that the prosperity of the wicked is only for a short time, Job undertakes to prove the very contrary, that in many instances their prosperity continues as long as they live, that they die in the midst of it, and that it is enjoyed by their posterity after them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the same turn in the argument: having in chapter 19 declared his belief in a retribution to come, Job now proceeds to traverse more directly Zophar's contention, and to show that even in this life there is not the retribution his friends had maintained there was.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the verse a man commending both his case and his discourse, both what he suffered and what he said, to the compassionate consideration of his friends. What he entreats is only fair: that they suffer him to speak and not break in upon him as Zophar had done. Losers, of all men, may have leave to speak; and if those who are accused and censured are not allowed to speak for themselves, they are wronged without remedy, and have no way to come at their right. He asks that they hear diligently and mark him, for we may as well not hear as not heed and observe what we hear. And his deepest plea is that his complaint is not to man but to God, before whom he and they stand upon even terms; it would be sad, Henry adds, if God should deal as unkindly with us as our friends sometimes do.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the map of the argument to come. Job expresses himself as puzzled by the dispensations of divine providence, because of the unequal distribution of temporal goods; he shows that wicked men often live long, prosper in their families, their flocks, and all their substance, and yet live in defiance of God and of sacred things; that at other times their prosperity is suddenly blasted, and they and their families come to ruin; and that God, too wise to err, deals out various lots to all according to his wisdom, some coming sooner and others later to the grave, while the wicked are reserved for a day of wrath. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job here plants his flag on the one stubborn fact his comforters will not own, that the wicked may flourish to the very end, and that the chapter which follows is the patient, grievous unfolding of it against the whole doctrine of retribution in this life.
2:
His first request is not for pity but for a hearing, and the witnesses gather around the strange bargain Job proposes, that attention itself shall stand in the place of comfort. The reformed John Gill takes "hear diligently my speech" as a plea for the closest attention to the oration he is about to deliver concerning the prosperity of wicked men, that his friends might the better weigh the force of his reasoning and the proof of facts he would give, and, if their minds were open to conviction, see their mistake and own that truth lay on his side. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the whole with the same economy: "Listen to my words, and let that be the consolation you give me."

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, set the request against the friends' failure. Far from being able to solve the enigma of Job's affliction, they do not once recognise the mystery as such, but cut the knot by wounding him with ever more frivolous accusations; therefore he entreats them to be at least willing to listen to his utterance respecting the unsolved riddle, and then (the imperative carrying its own consequence) this attention shall supply the place of their consolations, being comforting to him as their supposed comforts could never be. They are to bear with him, that is, without interruption to allow him to answer for himself.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press both the plea and a buried edge in it. John Wesley keeps it tender: "If you have no other comfort to administer, at least afford me this; and it will be a comfort to yourselves, in the reflection, to have dealt tenderly with your afflicted friend." Adam Clarke hears something sharper in the same word, for the noun rendered "consolations" he would read "retractations": let what I am about to say induce you to retract what you have said and recall your false judgments, since the Hebrew root signifies not only to comfort but to change one's mind and repent, which is why the Vulgate turned it "and repent," and Coverdale "and amend yourselves." Some, Clarke allows, take the verse ironically: I am now about to give you consolations for those you gave me; when I have done, turn them into mockery if you please. The witnesses do not divide over the request; they differ only in how much sting they hear beneath it, whether Job asks a simple hearing or already summons his comforters to unsay their charge.
3:
The plea for a hearing is renewed with a courtesy that is almost defiant, for Job grants his friends leave to mock once he has done. The reformed John Gill reads "suffer me that I may speak" as an entreaty for patience to hear him out to the end, not merely to begin; his friends might by their gestures seem as if they were breaking up and departing, or might raise a tumultuous clamour to hinder his reply, or break in upon him before he had finished as they had already done. Several of the Jewish commentators, Gill notes, render the word "bear me": though what he was going to say might sit heavy upon their minds, and be burdensome, grating, and uneasy to them, yet he entreats that they would endure it patiently until he had made an end of speaking.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the verse in their own rendering, "Suffer me, and I will speak, and after I have spoken thou mayest mock," and mark the sudden turn to the singular. The permission to scoff is granted not to the three together but to one, as if Job pointed at the last speaker who had provoked him; the magnanimity is real, but it is aimed. He asks only to finish, and will pay for the room to speak by surrendering the field afterward to whatever ridicule they please. The two imperatives, bear with me and then mock, frame the exchange as a fair contest with agreed rules, in which Job asks nothing for himself but the plain order of a just hearing, and stakes his whole vindication on being allowed to reach the end of his argument uninterrupted.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the two clauses in their bald simplicity: "Speak, without interruption. Mock, if I do not defend my cause with solid arguments, go on in your scoffs." The verse thus lays down the terms of the debate as a man sure of his ground would lay them: give me an unbroken hearing, and then, if my reasoning fails, jeer as you will. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job is not begging indulgence but claiming the barest justice of controversy, the right of the accused to state his whole case before sentence, for to be shouted down in the midst of a plea is, in any court, to be condemned without trial; and that the leave he so freely grants his mockers, so far from weakness, is the confidence of one who believes the facts he is about to marshal will silence the scoffing of themselves. It is the wager of a man who would rather be heard and derided than soothed and misjudged.
4:
Before the great catalogue of the wicked man's prosperity begins, Job pauses to say against whom his quarrel really lies, and the witnesses weigh the question "is my complaint to man?" The reformed John Gill answers it from the whole tenor of the book: Job had been complaining, and still was, but not to his friends nor to any other man; his complaint was made to God, of whom he thought himself hardly dealt with he could not tell why, and to whom he had appealed to know the reason of the contention. When his friends first came they said nothing to him, nor he to them; and when he did speak, it was to God, expostulating why he had ever been born, or had not died as soon as born.

The wesleyan-arminian voices hear in the verse the reasonableness of the sufferer's impatience. Adam Clarke renders the opening cry "Alas for me!" and turns it into a defence: is it not with a man that I speak? and if so, why should not my spirit be troubled? I do not reply against my Maker; I suffer much from God and man; why then may I not have the privilege of complaining to creatures like myself? John Wesley presses the same point plainly: "I do not make my complaint to, or expect relief from, you or any men, but from God only; and if my complaint were to man, have I not cause?"

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott draws the fullest paraphrase, and lifts the verse to the height of Job's boldness. It is not to man that he complains; he does not ask their sympathy, and therefore they need not resent an offence that is not given. But his complaint is to God, and concerning the ways of God he ventures to ask why it is that his justice is so tardy; and this, Ellicott adds, is the very problem which, when Job remembers it, troubles him, so that horror takes hold on his flesh, so difficult and arduous is it. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job here disclaims any grudge against his friends and carries his real controversy past them to heaven; his impatience is not the petulance of a man crossed by his equals but the anguish of one who cannot reconcile the delay of divine justice with the God he still addresses. The complaint is upward, and that is why it shakes him.
5:
Job asks his friends for a gesture rather than an argument, that they look at him and fall silent in astonishment. The reformed John Gill glosses "mark me" as "look at me," yet not at his person, which was no lovely sight, covered with boils from head to foot, his flesh clothed with worms and clods of dust, his skin scarce whole, a mere skeleton reduced to skin and bone; but at his sorrows and sufferings, that they might consider and contemplate them and see whether there was any sorrow like his, or any who suffered as he did in such pitiful circumstances; or that they would regard his words and well weigh what he was about to say concerning the providences of God toward good and bad men. The looking he asks is thus a double looking, at the wreck of his body and at the weight of his words, that from both together they might learn how ill his case answers to their easy rule.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the whole verse as a summons to stunned silence. Consider and compare, he has Job say, the state in which I was once with that in which I am now, and be astonished at the judgments and dispensations of God; you will then be confounded, you will put your hands upon your mouths and keep silent. And Clarke fills in the ancient sign: putting the hand on the mouth, or the finger on the lips, was the token of silence, so that the Egyptian god Harpocrates, the god of silence, is represented with his finger compressing his upper lip. The laying of the hand on the mouth is thus no vague image but the recognised posture of a man who owns himself out of his depth.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the sense compact: "Consider what I am about to say concerning the prosperity of the worst of men, and the pressures of some good men, and it is able to fill you with astonishment; lay your hand upon your mouth, be silent." The witnesses do not divide, and their agreement carries a rebuke that the gold standard of Job's own friends would later feel. Instead of expounding his troubles, they should have adored the unsearchable mysteries of a providence that afflicts a man of whom they know no evil; the fit response to what cannot be fathomed is not a confident verdict but the silent wonder of the hand upon the lip. Job asks his comforters to trade their too-ready explanations for the awe that his case ought to have taught them.
6:
The astonishment Job asks of his friends he first confesses in himself, for the very remembrance of his theme unmans him. The reformed John Gill runs through what the remembering may be: the iniquities of his youth he was made to possess, or his former state of prosperity reviewed against his present misery, or the evil tidings brought thick and fast of the loss of substance, servants, and children, so terrible and shocking; or, most likely here, the instances of providence he is about to relate in the verses that follow. Any way it be taken, the object of the remembering is a thing so heavy that it masters the body before the mouth can utter it, and it is enough, recalled, to shake him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry ties the trembling to the whole surprising strangeness of Job's case. When I remember that terrible day, Henry has him say, in which I was on a sudden stripped of all my comforts and stricken with sore boils, and when I remember all the hard speeches with which you have grieved me, I am afraid, and trembling takes hold of my flesh, especially when I compare this with the prosperous condition of many wicked people and the applause of their neighbours. And Henry draws the general note: the providences of God, in the government of the world, are sometimes very astonishing even to wise and good men, and bring them to their wits' end. It is not weakness but honesty that makes the mystery shake him, and no discredit to faith to be staggered by what it cannot yet explain.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses keep the confession close to the flesh. Adam Clarke has Job say, "I am about to speak of the mysterious workings of Providence, and I tremble at the thought of entering into a detail on such a subject; my very flesh trembles." John Wesley reduces it to a line: "The very remembrance of what is past fills me with dread and horror." The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the man who has just bidden his friends be astonished is himself the first to be astonished, that the riddle of the prospering wicked and the suffering righteous is no cool debating-point to him but a terror in the body; and that his trembling is itself an argument, for a thing that so shakes an upright man is not to be settled by the glib maxims his comforters keep repeating. The flesh recoils where the friends complacently explain.
7:
"Wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power?" With this question Job flings down the whole counter-thesis of his speech, and the witnesses read it as the flat contradiction of everything the friends have argued. The reformed John Gill hears it put either to God, as though Job could not reconcile it with the divine perfections that a holy and just Being should suffer such wretches to live upon his earth while a man who feared the Lord lay in heavy affliction; or else to the friends, whom he challenges to make so undeniable a fact comport with their own principle that only the wicked are grievously afflicted. Why, he asks, do the wicked live at all, even breathe, who breathe out nothing but sin, or rather why are they "lively," vigorous, and thriving?

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the verse into a direct thrust at the comforters: you have frequently asserted that the wicked are invariably punished in this life and the righteous distinguished by marks of God's kindness; how then does it come that many wicked men live long and prosperously, and at last die in peace, without any evidence of God's displeasure? This is a fact occurring daily; none can deny it; how then will you reconcile it with your maxims? The observation, Clarke insists, is enough of itself to overthrow their doctrine.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the three verbs as the height, breadth, and length of the wicked man's prosperity. They live and are not cut off by divine vengeance, but reprieved; they become old, living long enough to raise their families and estates, so that we read of a sinner a hundred years old; and they are mighty in power, preferred to places of authority, not only making a great figure but bearing a great sway. Then Henry asks the deeper why, and answers it. It is not because God has forsaken the earth, or does not see, or cannot punish; it is because the measure of their iniquities is not yet full. This is the day of God's patience, in which he even makes their prosperity serve his own counsels while it ripens them for ruin; but the chief reason is that he will make it appear there is another world which is the world of retribution, and not this. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the long life and high power of the ungodly is a fact too plain to deny, and that its very stubbornness demolishes the friends' arithmetic and points, past this world, to a judgment yet to come.
8:
The prosperity just asserted is now traced into the next generation, for "their seed is established in their sight." The reformed John Gill is careful that this is no seed sown in the earth but the wicked man's children: to have a numerous progeny was reckoned a great temporal blessing, and to see them settled happily an added one, and the crown of it was that the man beheld it with his own eyes while yet living, his offspring prospering near him, in the same neighbourhood, or even in like flourishing circumstances with himself. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same felicity: they see their own children grow up and become settled in the land, and behold their children's children also, so that their generations are not cut off, and even the posterity of the wicked continue.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the point into a direct rebuttal of the friends. Not only are the wicked mighty in power themselves, they leave their power to their children after them, a felicity the psalmist marks in the men of the world whose portion is in this life at Psalm 17:14; and this, Ellicott presses, flatly contradicts what Eliphaz had said at Job 15:34, what Bildad had said at Job 18:19, and what Zophar had said at Job 20:10. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, take the same clause as the head of the long strophe describing the wicked man's undisturbed household, the seed established before his eyes standing first because it is the very blessing the friends had denied him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a portrait of prosperity complete and consummate. They are multiplied, their family built up, and they have the satisfaction of seeing it; this, he says, is put first as that which gives both a pleasant enjoyment and a pleasing prospect. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the establishing of the wicked man's seed in his sight is not an incidental detail but the sharpest edge of Job's case, for it is precisely here that the friends had promised the hypocrite's line would be blotted out; and Job answers that, on the contrary, the ungodly often looks out from the midst of his wealth upon a settled and thriving posterity, and dies with that comfort unbroken. The very blessing the comforters made the mark of the righteous, Job shows resting daily on the heads of the ungodly.
9:
From the settled children Job turns to the untroubled house, for "their houses are safe from fear, neither is the rod of God upon them." The reformed John Gill unfolds the double security: safe from fear of enemies besetting or entering them, of thieves and robbers breaking in and carrying off their substance; or, reading the word as "peace," their families live in peace and prosperity among themselves, enjoying all good within doors and devoid of fear from anything without. The double freedom, Gill observes, is from the thing feared and from the fear itself, so that neither robber without nor dread within breaks the calm of the ungodly house. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the second clause: "neither is the rod of God upon them" means simply that they are not afflicted as other men, the very stroke Job himself was feeling being the stroke they escape; so plain a fact, he implies, needs no softening.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott again reads the verse as an open collision with the comforters. On the contrary, he observes, Zophar had just said that "a fire not blown should consume him" at Job 20:26, and Bildad that "destruction should dwell in his tabernacle, and brimstone be scattered upon his habitation" at Job 18:15; the friends had filled the wicked man's dwelling with terror and ruin, and Job answers by pointing to the wicked man's dwelling standing quiet and secure. Point for point he takes back what they had asserted.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the contrast most fully. Whereas Zophar had spoken of the wicked man's continual frights and terrors, Job says their houses are safe both from danger and from the fear of it, and so far are they from the killing wounds of God's sword or arrows that they do not feel the smart of so much as the rod of God upon them. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the second half of the verse is aimed like a dart at the friends' doctrine: they had made the trembling, haunted conscience the sure companion of ungodliness, and Job replies that the ungodly often sleep sound in houses that no fear disturbs and no rod visits. The rod of God, the very stroke Job feels in his own flesh, is precisely what these houses never feel; and that exemption, not any hidden merit, is what keeps them quiet. The peace the comforters promised only to the upright, Job finds spread as freely, and more freely, over the tents of men who never call on God at all.
10:
The prosperity that filled the house now overflows into the field and the fold, for "their bull gendereth, and faileth not; their cow calveth, and casteth not her calf." The reformed John Gill notes that after the wicked man's children and the peace within his doors, his happiness is here set forth by the increase of his cattle, one part put for the whole of his oxen and asses, camels and sheep, the very things in which the riches of men chiefly lay in those times and countries; a man was reckoned happy when these brought forth abundantly. The wealth of a patriarchal age, Gill notes, was counted in living stock, so that a teeming and untroubled herd was the very form prosperity took. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the plain sense of the breeding: the bull passes over the cow and fails not, their flocks multiply greatly, they bring forth in due time, and none of them is barren.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch labour the philology of the two Hebrew words, and defend the natural reading against a learned emendation. The word for "his bull" is undoubtedly the male, they argue, and the verb means to gender or impregnate, not, as Rosenmuller after Bochart had urged on the authority of the Septuagint and Jerome, to be understood of the female that conceives; for the root, even in its simplest stem, carries the sense of impregnating, which is why the Targum renders it by a word meaning "impregnating." The point is small, but it secures the picture: the beasts breed without mishap, the herd grows, and nothing miscarries.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the third mark of a complete prosperity, that they are rich and thrive in their estates; of this he gives but one instance, that their cattle increase and they meet with no disappointment in them, not so much as a cow casting her calf, so that their much must needs grow more, the very fruitfulness that was promised to obedience at Exodus 23:26 and Deuteronomy 7:14. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job piles the homely evidence high on purpose: the very blessing of unbroken increase which the law annexed to faithfulness, and which the friends would confine to the godly, is seen resting daily on the fields of men who defy God; the wicked man's herd multiplies as surely as the righteous man's, and the ledger of his wealth shows no red mark of heaven's displeasure. The blessing of the fruitful field, pledged in the law to the obedient, falls here on the disobedient, and falls without fail.
11:
From the breeding herds Job passes to the swarming nursery, for the wicked "send forth their little ones like a flock, and their children dance." The reformed John Gill will not have the flock be literal lambs but the man's own increasing family, likened for its numbers to a flock of sheep, those most multiplying and numerous of creatures. The sending forth he takes either of the children being born and proceeding from their parents as plants out of the earth or branches from a tree, or of their being let loose, not to school to be taught useful learning, but into the streets to play and pipe and dance; and he hears in the phrase a note of their being left wholly to themselves, at liberty to do as they please, under no restraint and no care taken for their sober and virtuous upbringing. The very looseness of the picture, children turned out into the streets to pipe and dance, is for Gill part of its meaning, a prosperity so secure that it takes no thought for the morrow of its own offspring.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is content to leave the reference open. It is not very clear, he says, whether the little ones are the young of the flocks or the children of the house; the first clause may mean the one and the next clause the other, so that while the young of their cattle are gathered in flocks, their numerous children are healthy and vigorous and dance for joy. Either way the impression is of abundant, careless life, teeming and glad.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the fourth feature of the wicked man's felicity, that they are merry and live a jovial life, sending forth their little ones abroad among their neighbours in great numbers to sport themselves, with dancing that is fittest for children, whose innocency guards them against the mischiefs that commonly attend it. Yet Henry hears in the scene an instance of vanity as well as of prosperity, for here is none of that care Abraham took of his household, to teach them the way of the Lord at Genesis 18:19; these children do not pray or learn their catechism but dance and sing. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job holds up the laughing, dancing broods of the ungodly as one more proof that heaven's rod is not on them, and that the very carelessness of the sight, children raised for pleasure and not for God, is at once the measure of the family's ease and the seed of its ruin.
12:
The dancing children are matched by the music of their parents, for "they take the timbrel and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ." The reformed John Gill assigns the instruments to the parents rather than the little ones: they took the timbrel and harp into their hands and played while their children danced, and so spent their time merrily; or, as Jarchi and Aben Ezra read it, they lifted up the voice with tabret and harp, joining vocal and instrumental music together to make the greater harmony and the greater pleasure. It is a household given wholly to mirth.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the antique instruments. The verb, he says, may mean that they rise up or lift themselves, alluding to the rural exercise of dancing; the timbrel is a kind of drum, like the tom-tom of the Asiatics; the harp is something of the stringed kind; and the word rendered "organ" means nothing like the modern instrument, but rather the syrinx or pipe of several unequal reeds that gives a shrill and lively sound. Clarke commends Mr. Good's rendering, "They trip merrily to the sound of the pipe," and quotes the verses of glancing, twinkling feet that catch the true notion of rustic gambols at festival. Then he drives the sting home: let it be observed that all this is spoken of the children of those very people who say to God, "Depart from us; what is the Almighty, that we should serve him?" Is it any wonder that the children of such parents should be living to the flesh, when neither they nor their parents know God nor pray unto him?

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the same picture and the same moral. Though the parents are not so youthful as to dance themselves, they take the timbrel and harp and pipe, and their children dance after their pipe, and they know no grief to put their instruments out of tune or withhold their hearts from any joy; sensual pleasures are all the delights of carnal people, and as the men are themselves, so they breed their children. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the song and dance of the ungodly house is no idle ornament in Job's argument but part of its force: here is prosperity so unbroken that it breaks into music, and a mirth so untroubled that it can be handed down to the next generation, all in families that have shut God out; the untuned harp of the afflicted righteous, meanwhile, hangs on the willows.
13:
"They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave." Here the witnesses meet a real difference over the Hebrew, though they agree on the terrible ease of the death described. The reformed John Gill reads "in wealth" as "in good," not the good of holy living but of earthly enjoyment; such men place all their happiness in worldly good and spend all their days in getting or enjoying it, in no spiritual exercise of prayer or praise, public or private. He then flags the textual point: "we follow the Keri or margin" in reading that they spend their days, but the Cetib, the written text, is that they "become old," wearing out their years in prosperity to the very end.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke weighs the same variant at length and comes down the other way. The consonantal text, he says, has a word meaning "they grow old" or wear out as with age, while the margin reads "they consume" or spend; the Masora counts it among the eleven words written with one letter and read with another. Clarke inclines to "they grow old," because Job's argument gains considerable strength from it: they not only fare sumptuously every day, but even wear out and grow old in that life, and are not cut off by any sudden judgment of God; therefore the friends' doctrine, that the wicked are cut off suddenly and have but a short time, is far from the truth. So a genuine debate stands in the verse, whether the wicked "spend" their prosperous days or "grow old" in them, with Clarke preferring the reading that most sharpens Job's case.

On the death itself the witnesses are one. Keil and Delitzsch render the line, "they enjoy their days in prosperity, and in a moment go down to Sehol," the descent sudden and painless. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the sting of "in a moment": they go down to death without being made to feel the lingering tortures that Job had to undergo. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same in a breath: "they do not die of a lingering and tormenting disease." Both Clarke and the others note the paradox that, if there were no life after this, such a death, quick and without previous alarm, were the most desirable of all. The witnesses do not divide over the point that matters most: the wicked man wears out a whole life of wealth and then slips into the grave as into sleep, spared the very agony under which Job, the upright man, lies groaning; and that contrast, not any sudden stroke of vengeance, is the fact the comforters must answer.
14:
The ease of their life issues not in gratitude but in defiance, for these prospering men "say unto God, Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways." The reformed John Gill traces the insolence to the wealth itself, which has this tendency, to make men proud and to forsake and lightly esteem their Creator and benefactor, even to set their mouths against him and speak contemptuously of him; and he adds the sober qualification that though the words may not always be openly uttered, they are conceived in the mind and inwardly spoken, and abundantly proclaimed by the men's lives and conversations. The heart's speech and the life's speech, Gill insists, say the same thing, so that the blasphemy is real whether or not the lips ever frame it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects the connective and, with it, the logic. "Therefore they say unto God" should rather be "Yet they said unto God, Depart from us"; the point is not that prosperity naturally leads to this speech but that, in the teeth of such prosperity received from God's hand, they turn and bid him be gone. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, render the whole with the same adversative force, "and yet they said to God, Depart from us, we desire not the knowledge of thy ways," so that the atheism stands out the more monstrous against the mercies that provoke it. The corrected reading, on their view, makes the sin not a slow drift into forgetfulness but a direct affront, flung back in the very face of the Giver.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses expound the speech itself. Adam Clarke calls it the language of their conduct, though not directly of their lips: "Let us alone; we do not trouble thee; thy ways are painful, we do not like cross-bearing; thy ways are spiritual, we wish to live after the flesh; we have learned to do our own will, and do not wish to study thine." John Wesley agrees that they say it "sometimes in words, but commonly in their thoughts and the language of their lives," and roots it in "their constant prosperity." The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the sharpest scandal of the chapter is not merely that the wicked prosper but that their prosperity hardens them into an open dismissal of the very God who feeds them; and Ellicott's "yet" is the hinge of it, for the gifts that ought to draw men to their Giver are here turned into the ground for driving him away. The bounty is real, and so is the blasphemy that answers it.
15:
"What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? and what profit should we have, if we pray unto him?" The witnesses hear in this pair of questions the two great bonds of religion, duty and interest, deliberately cut. The reformed John Gill probes the first: what is there in God, in his nature and perfections, that should oblige us to serve him? One would think the very name "Almighty," which they own, enough to engage it, since he is able to save and to destroy, even to destroy body and soul in hell; but fulness of riches and power swells the mind with pride and puts men on asking such questions. The question, Gill says, is full of atheism, suggesting there is nothing in God worthy of regard, as if he were a mere idol, doing neither good nor evil, having forsaken the earth and taking no notice of the affairs of men.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the speech its cool, worldly voice. What allegiance do we owe him? we feel no obligation to obey; and what profit can we derive from prayer? We are as happy as flesh and blood can make us; our kingdom is of this world; we wish for no other portion than that which we have. And Clarke turns the taunt back on the taunters: those who have never prayed as they ought know nothing of the benefits of prayer, and so pronounce it profitless out of sheer ignorance of what it is.

The two questions, the witnesses agree, echo an older defiance. As Pharaoh had asked, "Who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice?" at Exodus 5:2, so these speak slightingly of God, as of a mere name or cipher with whom they have nothing to do; hardly of religion, which they call a "service" and mean a drudgery; and highly of themselves, who are rich and mighty and think it beneath them to be accountable. They will not believe it their duty to be religious, nor their interest, since prayer, as they reckon, pays no debts and portions no children; it is vain to serve God, they say with the men of Malachi 3:14. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that here the prosperity of the wicked reaches its darkest fruit, a settled contempt of God grounded on the very abundance he has given; and that the blasphemy exposes the friends' scheme, for these open despisers of the Almighty are the men who flourish, while the God-fearing Job lies in the dust.
16:
Job will not leave the blasphemy of the wicked without disowning it, and the verse turns from their speech to his own verdict: "Lo, their good is not in their hand; the counsel of the wicked is far from me." The reformed John Gill reads the first clause as a check upon their pride: though their good is in their possession for the present, it is not in the power of their hands to keep, nor to carry with them when they die; God who gave it can take it away, and therefore it might well have profited them to serve him and pray to him. The wealth they boast is a loan, not a freehold.

The grammatical-historical voices make the clause the very statement of the mystery. Keil and Delitzsch take the particle as introducing the true relation of things: their prosperity is not by their own hand, not their own work but a gift from above, the gift even of the God whom they so shamelessly deny; and that God should grant such great and lasting prosperity to such men is precisely the enigma Job cannot bring to view, though his abhorrence of their impiety is in no way lessened by it. Charles Ellicott agrees that their good, being not in their own hand, constitutes the very mystery of it, for it is God who gives it to them; though he allows the words might instead be read as a supposed objection, "Lo, thou repliest, their prosperity is not in their hand," with the closing line then Job's indignant repudiation of all fellowship with their reasoning.

On that closing line the witnesses gather as one. Keil and Delitzsch render "the counsel of the wicked be far from me" as Job's disavowal, be it far from me to speak or think according to their way of mind. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the same, "Far be it from me to advocate the cause of the wicked; I have nothing in common with them; I state a fact, that they are often found in continual prosperity, and another fact, that they are often found in misery," but he is no apologist for the men whose lot he describes. John Wesley draws the moral together: wicked men have no reason to reject God because of their prosperity, for their wealth is not obtained nor kept by their own might but only by God's power and favour, and therefore Job is far from approving their opinion or following their course. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job, even while he presses the scandal of the prospering wicked to its height, sets the widest distance between himself and their contempt of God, owning the very hand they deny.
17:
"How oft is the candle of the wicked put out?" Job now takes up the friends' own image and turns it into a question, and the witnesses divide over how the question is meant. The reformed John Gill notes that Job returns here to his account of the settled prosperity of wicked men, taking up Bildad's word that the candle of the wicked should be put out and asking how often that is really seen; by the candle he means not the soul, which cannot be extinguished, but either the natural life or, rather, the outward prosperity and happiness of the ungodly, and he asks whether the instances of its being snuffed out are frequent or few.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears a plain challenge to the comforters: tell me how often you see the candle of the wicked put out; do you not as often see it burnt down to the socket until it goes out of itself, and see their mirth and prosperity continuing to the last? Perhaps there are as many instances of notorious sinners ending their days in pomp as ending them in misery, an observation enough to invalidate the friends' arguments and show that no certain judgment of a man's character can be made from his outward condition. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the line as a measured concession: "I grant that this happens often, though not constantly, as you affirm," the lamp being the wicked man's glory and outward happiness.

Here the grammatical-historical voices open a genuine debate. Charles Ellicott offers two constructions: either this verse and the next are a concession, Job granting "I admit it is as you say with the wicked," or they should be read interrogatively, "How often is it that we do see this?", with the implied answer, seldom. Keil and Delitzsch take the second road firmly, rendering "How rarely is the light of the wicked put out, and their calamity breaketh in upon them, that God distributeth snares in his wrath." So the schools part over the very tone of the question, whether it is a candid admission that the wicked are sometimes cut off, or a rhetorical "how seldom!" that all but denies it. On the sequel the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the concessive sense, granting that oftentimes the rejoicing of the wicked is short and his seed cut off, and that in his anger God portions out to each his due share of misery. The witnesses do not finally divide on Job's aim, that the friends' rule of swift ruin fails the test of experience; they differ only on whether he grants the exception or, with Keil and Delitzsch, all but withdraws it.
18:
The image of the snuffed candle passes into that of the wind-driven chaff, for the wicked, when they do fall, "are as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carrieth away." The reformed John Gill keeps the interrogative running from the verse before: how often are they as stubble before the wind, how often does God so deal with them that they become as chaff before the storm? The question, on his reading, still presses the rarity of such sudden overthrow against the friends' confident rule; on that construction the whole verse hangs on the suppressed "how often," so that even the wicked man's ruin, when it does come, is numbered among the rare cases and not the settled rule.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears behind the words the winnowing of judgment, and cannot help recalling the Baptist's threshing-floor, the fan in the hand that thoroughly purges the floor and burns the chaff with unquenchable fire, so that the wicked shall not stand in the judgment but be like the chaff which the wind driveth away. Were the thought not so common, he says, he would have supposed the writer borrowed it from Psalm 1:4; the Hebrew, he adds, pictures men carried off by a furious storm, and borne away as booty is by the swift-riding robbers of the desert, who fall on their prey and are gone. The comparison, Clarke grants, is a commonplace of Scripture, which only shows how naturally the wind-blown chaff figures the end of the ungodly when at last it comes.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse in the same figure, the wicked as straw before the wind and chaff the whirlwind sweeps away, and set it within the movement of Job's argument as he presses toward the question that follows. For the whole point of the friends' position, they observe, is that virtue is necessarily and constantly rewarded with prosperity and sin with misfortune; and it is against that inflexible law, not against God's justice as such, that Job is contending. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job does not deny the wicked are as chaff, light, worthless, and continually exposed to ruin; he denies only that the wind falls on them as regularly and as promptly as his comforters require. They are chaff indeed, but chaff the storm often spares for years. In the height of their pomp there is indeed but a step between them and destruction, yet the step is often long deferred, and it is that deferral, not the final frailty, which the friends cannot explain and Job will not let them evade.
19:
The friends had a ready answer to the wicked man's long impunity, that God stores up the reckoning for his children, and the verse gives it: "God layeth up his iniquity for his children." But the witnesses divide sharply over whose voice this is. The reformed John Gill takes it as an objection Job foresees and grants: be it so that the wicked prosper undisturbed in their own persons, yet God reserves the punishment of their iniquity for their children, and this, Gill says, Job allows, for God does take notice of men's sins, lays them up in the book of his remembrance, and visits them on the posterity when the measure is full.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same clause the opposite way, as the hypothetical reply of Job's antagonists put into his own mouth, with the second half of the verse his sharp retort: "Let him repay it to himself, that he may know it." Keil and Delitzsch take exactly this course, printing the first line as the friends' maxim, "Eloah layeth up his iniquity for his children!", and the rest as Job's answer, "may he recompense it to the man himself that he may feel it, may his own eyes see his ruin." So a real debate stands in the verse: is the storing-up of guilt for the children Job's own concession to the friends' doctrine, or is it their doctrine which he quotes only to reject, demanding that the sinner, not his innocent sons, be made to feel the stroke?

The other witnesses expound the friends' principle without settling the question of voice. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry states it in its own terms: the oppressor lays up his goods for his children to make them gentlemen, but God lays up his iniquity for them to make them beggars, keeping an exact account of the fathers' sins, sealing them among his treasures as at Deuteronomy 32:34, and justly punishing the children while the cursed riches are found as assets in their hands. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke grounds it in the second commandment at Exodus 20:5, visiting the fathers' iniquity on the children who copy their example or inherit their ill-gotten goods; John Wesley reads "layeth up" as a treasuring of wrath against the day of wrath, as at Romans 2:5, God punishing the sinner both in his person and in his posterity. The witnesses do not resolve the crux, but the debate itself carries Job's true point: the friends' appeal to a delayed, transferred punishment is precisely what he finds too easy, for justice deferred to the children leaves the guilty man himself untouched.
20:
Against a punishment postponed to the children, Job sets a demand that the sinner himself be made to see and taste it, for "his eyes shall see his destruction, and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty." The reformed John Gill reads the verbs as Job's wish and argument: his eyes should see his own destruction, for otherwise it will not touch him; only when a man has personal experience of affliction as the punishment of his sin, or with his own eyes sees his children in distress on his account, does the stroke sensibly affect him, as it did Zedekiah, whose children were slain before his eyes.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch put the whole weight on the pronouns. The rare word for "destruction" means properly a blow or thrust, hence ruin; and the emphasis, they insist, lies on the signs of the person in "his own eyes" and "let him drink": rather may the sinner's own eyes see his ruin, may he himself have to drink of the divine wrath, than that it be laid up for his sons; for what interest, the following verse asks, has he in his house after him? The cup of wrath they take in the sense worked out by Asaph at Psalm 75:9 and carried on by the prophets and the seer of the Revelation. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, reads the verse the same way, as the continuation of Job's suggested amendment of the divine government: his own eyes should see his destruction, and he should drink of the wrath, since he has no concern in his house once his own months are cut off.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the terror personal and present. His eyes shall see his destruction, he says, means the sinner shall perceive its approach and bear the double punishment of fearing and feeling, a thousand deaths in the fear of one; and the cup of God's wrath, so often named in Scripture, as at Jeremiah 25:15, he likens to the cup of poison a criminal was made to drink, the very death assigned to Socrates. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the drinking of the wrath to the world to come, where the eyes wilfully shut against the grace of God shall be opened to see his destruction. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job's whole reply to the friends' delayed vengeance is a demand for justice that the sinner himself can feel, seen with his own eyes and drunk from his own cup; a punishment that only falls after he is dead and gone is, to Job, no punishment of him at all.
21:
The reason Job presses for a reckoning the sinner himself can feel is given here: "for what pleasure hath he in his house after him, when the number of his months is cut off in the midst?" The reformed John Gill unfolds the indifference both ways. As the prosperity of his children after his death gives the dead man no pleasure, so their calamities and distresses give him no pain; he knows nothing of what befalls his family, it is no part of his concern, and he can feel neither their happiness as a blessing nor their ruin as a punishment to himself. What business, Gill asks with the Hebrew, has he with his house after death? The affairs of his family do not touch him at all.

The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen the same thought. Adam Clarke reads it that whatever may happen to his posterity the sinner neither knows nor cares, being now numbered with the dead, and that before his time, his months cut off in the midst; he even notes an alternative turn, "behold how speedily God destroys the house of the wicked after him, how he shortens the number of his months." John Wesley presses the argument against the friends directly: what delight can you take in the thought of the wicked man's posterity being punished, when he himself is dying an untimely death, that number of months which by the course of nature he might have lived being cut off by violence and beyond his feeling?

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lets the New Testament illustrate the point. Our Saviour has shown how little pleasure the rich man in hell had in his house after him, when the memory of the good things received in his lifetime would not cool his tongue but added to his misery, and the fear that his five brethren should follow him only deepened it, at Luke 16:25; so little will the gain of the world profit the man who has lost his soul. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that this verse is the nerve of Job's whole answer to the doctrine of deferred punishment: a stroke that lands only on a man's household after he is dead reaches nothing of the man, for the grave has cut every cord of interest between him and his house; if God's justice is to be felt as justice, it must find the sinner while he yet has eyes to see and a cup to drink.
22:
Having pressed his own hard question, Job checks himself and all disputants with a reminder of who is on trial: "shall any teach God knowledge, seeing he judgeth those that are high?" The reformed John Gill hears the rebuke aimed at every presumption, his own included: who shall take upon him to instruct the God of knowledge in the path of judgment, to tell him whom he shall afflict and whom spare, and when and how? Shall his dealings in providence be made the criterion of men's characters, as if love and hatred could be read off from outward events, so that God must be schooled in what he ought to do? These things are to be left to him who does all after the counsel of his own will.

The wesleyan-arminian voices read the verse as the door shut on all such arrogance. Adam Clarke asks who among the sons of men can pretend to teach God how to govern the world, who himself teaches those that are high, the heavenly inhabitants that excel us infinitely in knowledge and wisdom; neither angels nor men can comprehend the reasons of the divine providence, a depth known only to God. John Wesley turns the point straight against the friends: you teach God how to govern the world, when you tell him he must not afflict the godly nor give the wicked prosperity, but must invariably punish the one and reward the other in this life; no, he will act as sovereign, and with great variety, for the highest persons on earth he exactly knows and gives sentence on them as he sees fit.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott suggests that the words may be regarded as the hypothetical reply of Job's antagonist, thrown in and then answered, though he leaves the reader free to construe them otherwise. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry resolves the whole difference of the wicked man's varying fate into the wisdom and sovereignty of God: dare we arraign his proceedings, or tell him which sinner to spare and which to punish? He judges those that are high, angels and princes alike, and will himself be accountable to none; he is the Judge of all the earth and will do right, as at Genesis 18:25 and Romans 3:6. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that here Job lifts the whole dispute above the friends' tidy equations: the unequal lots of men are not a ledger for us to audit but the acts of a sovereign Judge whose reasons lie beyond the reach of angels, and whose government it is folly, and the friends' peculiar folly, to presume to correct.
23:
"One dieth in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet." To prove that outward lot decides nothing of a man's standing with God, Job sets two deaths side by side, and the witnesses begin with the man cut off in his prime. The reformed John Gill dwells on the strangeness of it: man comes to his full strength only by slow degrees, and often loses it through a train of diseases, yet here death seizes him in the very fulness of his vigour, no strength of man being any security against it; the words may even be rendered "in the strength of his integrity" or perfection, in his very completeness. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states the design plainly: Job enlarges on the inequality of human fate, showing that death is the only equaliser.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, render the pair that runs through these verses, "one dieth in his full strength, being still cheerful and free from care," his troughs full of milk and the marrow of his bones well watered, while "another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and hath not enjoyed wealth," and both at last lie together in the dust with the worms covering them. The whole point of the parallel, they note, is that the manner of a man's death, easy or bitter, is no index of his character before God.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gathers the four verses into one lesson: the inequality of fortune, goods, health, and strength decides nothing either for or against a man in reference to the approbation of God, since these various lots are no indication of wickedness or innocence; one has a sudden, another a lingering death, but by none of these can the eternal state be determined. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fills in the ease of this first death: the man is wholly at ease and quiet, under no apprehension of death's approach, healthful and vigorous and of a good constitution, counting on many years of mirth, and yet cut off in a moment; it is a common thing, Henry warns, for men to be taken away in the highest degree of health, when they least expect it and think themselves best armed against it. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job's first specimen, the strong man dying carefree in the fulness of his powers, is aimed straight at the friends: if a serene and painless death crowned only the righteous, this ease would prove the man good, but it proves nothing, for death takes the vigorous sinner as gently as any saint.
24:
The carefree death of the strong man is drawn out in a line whose very words the witnesses find obscure: "his breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moistened with marrow." The reformed John Gill reports the difficulty at once. Since the figure is not literally true of men, some versions read "his bowels" or "his sides are full of fat," the words for side and fat lying near in sound; but the term may signify vessels for liquids, whence Mr. Broughton's "his pails are full of milk." Either way it paints a man plump, sleek, and vigorous when death lays hold of him, not wasted by consumption or pining sickness, enjoying rivers of milk and a large increase, the very opposite of the wasting Zophar had threatened.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke labours the single strange word, which occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible and is most likely a provincial term now lost. Following Parkhurst, he takes it as a noun meaning the bowels or intestines, so that the clause reads "his intestines are full of fat," the rendering of the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and others; he mentions Mr. Good's conjecture of that sleekness of skin which fatness gives, but doubts it, and offers his own guess that the word may denote the involutions of the inward parts. The uncertainty, he freely owns, is real.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the same crux and leans a third way. The word is uncertain, occurring only here; some understand it literally of milk-pails, others of the lacteal vessels of the human body, and this last, he judges, certainly suits the parallelism better, balancing the marrow in the bones of the second line. So a genuine debate stands over the hapax: is it the milk-pails of a rich man's dairy, the fat-filled bowels of a well-fed body, or the lacteals that answer to the moistened marrow? The witnesses do not divide over the picture the line conveys, of a body in the pink of health and abundance at the very hour of death, but they cannot agree on the anatomy of the metaphor. What none of them doubts is its use in Job's argument: the man who dies fat, sleek, and well-nourished is the wicked man of the friends' own portrait, dying not under a rod but in the bloom of prosperity, so that his easy end is one more witness that the outward lot proves nothing.
25:
"And another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and never eateth with pleasure." Against the sleek and carefree death Job now sets its opposite, and the witnesses mark that this too may be a wicked man, so that the contrast lies not between saint and sinner but within the ranks of men whose lot tells nothing of their standing. The reformed John Gill reads it so: there is a difference among wicked men, some happy in life and in the circumstances of their death, others unhappy in both, their life a scene of afflictions that embitter it, dying in bitter pains and agonies of body, in distress and horror of mind and black despair, as Judas and such as he.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes the same view of the sufferer: "another wicked man," for there is great variety in God's dispensations, who distributes great prosperity to one and great affliction to another according to his wise but secret counsel. The point is not that the bitter death marks the worse man, but that the two deaths fall without regard to desert. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, render the line within their pairing, "another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and hath not enjoyed wealth," the man going down never having tasted the good of life, in flat antithesis to the other's abundance.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the bitter death an echo of Job's own case, for this is a man such as poor Job was himself now in, dying with a great deal of previous pain and misery, in the bitterness of his soul, and never eating with pleasure, having no appetite for his food nor any relish of it through sickness, age, or sorrow of mind. What great reason, Henry adds, have those to be thankful who are in health and eat with pleasure, and what little reason to complain who sometimes do not, when many never do. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job has now completed his pair: one man dies at ease in his strength, another in anguish with a wasted appetite, and both descend from lives that gave no sure sign of God's favour or wrath; and the second death, so like Job's own present misery, quietly presses the question whether his bitterness proves him the sinner his friends suppose, or only proves that the lots of men are dealt by a counsel too deep for their reading.
26:
The two deaths meet in one bed, for however differently men die, "they shall lie down alike in the dust, and the worms shall cover them." The reformed John Gill reads it of all alike, those who lived and died in prosperity and those in bitterer circumstances: death levels them and brings them into the same state, laid on dusty beds where there is no difference, their rest together in the dust, until they are awakened in the morning of the resurrection. The bed of dust makes no distinction of estate, and the same worms feed on the one as on the other. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says the same with a plainer edge: death levels all distinctions and the grave makes all equal; there may be a difference in the grave itself, splendid monuments enshrining corruption, but the human corpse is the same in all, and the sod must lie as close upon the one as upon the other.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses how this equality compounds the mystery. Not only is the inequality of the wicked man's life a stumbling-block, he observes, but so also is the equality which obliterates all distinction between them in death; the very grave that ought to redress the imbalance only confirms it, for the fat and carefree sinner and the bitter and wasted one come to the identical dust. The problem, in other words, is not solved by mortality but doubled by it, for the grave, which the friends might have pleaded as the great redresser, only ratifies the inequity of the life.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the moral the others imply: all these worldly differences are ended by death, and men lie in the grave without any distinction, so that no man can tell who is good and who is bad by the events that befall them in this life. And he adds the sombre reach of it beyond the grave, that if one wicked man die in a palace and another in a dungeon, they will meet in the congregation of the dead, and the worm that dieth not and the fire that is not quenched will be the same to both, which makes such differences not worth perplexing ourselves about. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job's argument has reached its floor: the friends had read a man's destiny in his outward lot, but the dust reads the same over prince and pauper, over the sleek sinner and the sighing one, and the levelling of the grave, so far from vindicating their doctrine, buries it. What death makes equal, Wesley warns, it does not thereby explain, and forbids us to read any man's eternal state from the manner of his end.
27:
Job now names aloud what he knows his friends are thinking, for "behold, I know your thoughts, and the devices which ye wrongfully imagine against me." The reformed John Gill grants that the searching of thoughts is God's own prerogative, the Lord alone being the searcher of hearts, but allows that a wise and observant man may make shrewd guesses from hints and half-words, from the index of the countenance and the gestures of the body; and thus Job knew that his friends' judgments differed from his, and that for all his proof they remained unconvinced. The reading of hearts, Gill grants, is God's alone, yet enough of the mind leaks out through look and word for a watchful man to know when he is disbelieved. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts the read thought in a sentence: "ye still think that because I am grievously afflicted, I must therefore be a felonious transgressor."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse with a keener word, "behold, I know your thoughts and the stratagems with which ye overpower me," and identify the secret thought Job sees through: it is their fixed suspicion that he is such an evil-doer as he has been describing, reaping in his ruin the just reward of his deeds. The devices are not idle musings but a strategy of insinuation; the word they choose, "stratagems," turns the friends' comfort into a campaign, a settled plan of attack that Job has detected and now announces he has seen to the bottom of.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears Job answering an argument he can feel coming. He knows they will not agree with him, for their judgments are tinctured by their prejudice against him and by the devices they wrongfully imagine against his comfort and honour; and how, Henry asks, can such men be convinced? The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds that Job knows their discourses, though framed of wicked men in general, are particularly levelled at him. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that with this verse the debate becomes personal and open: Job strips the courtesy from the friends' generalities and lays bare the syllogism hidden in them, that the afflicted must be the guilty, and that he, being afflicted beyond all of them, must be the chief transgressor. He has heard the unspoken verdict, and the verses that follow will drag it into the light to answer it. The courtesy is over; the charge so long insinuated is now spoken aloud, that it may at last be met.
28:
The unspoken charge Job now quotes in the friends' own mouths: "for ye say, Where is the house of the prince? and where are the dwelling places of the wicked?" The reformed John Gill reads it as the very words forming on their lips, what they are about to say next, the confident appeal to the ruined mansions of great oppressors as proof that God does not let the wicked stand. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, render it "where is the house of the tyrant, and where the pavilions of the wicked?", taking the friends to point at the vanished dwellings of overbearing men as their standing evidence. The ruined pavilion of the tyrant, they had assumed, was proof enough that God overthrows the wicked in this present life.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the logic of the taunt: to prove your point, you ask, Where is the house of the tyrant and oppressor? Are they not overthrown and destroyed? and is not that a proof that God does not permit the wicked to enjoy prosperity? The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, reads the word "prince" as its own key, taking it of the generous, virtuous, princely man set in antithesis to the wicked, and hears the friends insinuating a dilemma against Job: how can we tell who is virtuous and who is wicked, and to which sort do you belong? All along, Ellicott notes, they had hinted that though he seemed righteous he was really wicked, and here they press the innuendo home; the question, on his reading, is a trap, for unable to point to any open crime in Job they make his calamity itself the evidence of a hidden one.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry brings the question to its sharpest personal point. The friends were ready, in answer to Job's account of the prospering wicked, to ask, Where is the house of the prince? that is, where now is Job's own house, and the house of his eldest son in which his children were feasting? Inquire into the ruined circumstances of Job's house and family, they imply, and compare them with the doom of tyrants and oppressors, and you will conclude that Job is such a one. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that this is the friends' whole case compressed into a question, the argument from Job's fallen estate to Job's hidden guilt; and by quoting it so exactly Job has already begun to dismantle it, setting it up to be answered, for the next verses will summon the testimony of all who travel the roads of the world to overturn the very inference the comforters think so plain.
29:
To the friends' confident question Job answers with an appeal to common witness: "have ye not asked them that go by the way? and do ye not know their tokens?" The reformed John Gill takes the travellers as any wayfarers met on the road, of whom one might ask the true state and character of men and of Job himself, and learn what was really thought of the case. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes the appeal Job's own rejoinder: consult travellers who have gone through different countries, and they will tell you they have seen both examples, the wicked in great prosperity in some instances and suddenly destroyed in others; had the friends made proper inquiry, they would have heard of the wicked man's peaceful end in a thousand instances as well as of his ruin.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott glosses the "tokens" as the marks and evidences of the travellers' experience, the conclusions at which observant men who have seen the world have arrived; Job stakes his case not on his own solitary view but on the accumulated report of all who have watched the ways of providence. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the point to its widest: he means any person that passes along the highway, every one you meet with, for it is so common a thing that no man of common sense is ignorant of it, and the tokens are the examples and evidences of this truth that such travellers can produce.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the appeal into doctrine. So confident is Job that he is willing to refer the cause to the next man that comes by; turn to whichever of the children of men you will, and you will find them all of his mind, that the punishment of sinners is designed more for the other world than for this, according to the ancient prophecy of Enoch, the seventh from Adam, cited at Jude 14, and that the workers of iniquity often flourish only that they may be destroyed for ever, as at Psalm 92:7. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job meets the friends' narrow specimen of ruined tyrants with the broad testimony of mankind, the pooled observation of all who travel and watch; and that this common witness runs against the comforters, for it reports the wicked as often spared as struck, and so points, past this uneven world, to a judgment yet to come.
30:
The tokens the travellers report come to this, "that the wicked is reserved to the day of destruction; they shall be brought forth to the day of wrath." The reformed John Gill reads the reserving as a sparing: the wicked are withheld and kept from many of the calamities that fall on others, and so are reserved, either to a time of greater destruction in this life or, rather, to eternal destruction in the world to come, the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men, when they shall be destroyed body and soul in hell. As the fallen angels are kept in chains of darkness unto that same day, so the wicked, fitted by their own sins for destruction, are kept by God's providence unto it, as condemned malefactors reserved for execution. The sparing, on his reading, is the most dangerous of mercies, a keeping-back that only heaps up the final account.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the plain moral against the friends' rule: though every one can tell that he has seen the wicked in prosperity, and even spend a long life in it, this is no proof that God loves him or that he shall be happy in the next world; there he shall meet the day of wrath, there the wicked shall be punished and the just rewarded. Long life in sin, Clarke insists, is no token of God's love; prosperity here settles nothing, for the reckoning is elsewhere. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voice, render the travellers' testimony in the same key, that the wicked was spared in the day of calamity and in the day of the outbursts of wrath were led away, the very exemption in this life pointing on to a wrath deferred.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley marks a small turn in the grammar, that Job speaks of the same person but changes the singular to the plural, possibly to intimate that although for the present only some wicked men are punished, yet in that day all of them shall suffer, brought forth as malefactors are brought from prison to execution. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that this verse is the heart of Job's answer to the friends' appeal to ruined houses: the wicked man's escape from present calamity is no acquittal but a respite, a keeping-back for the day of wrath; and that this, the settled report of all who observe the world, overturns the comforters' inference from Job's fallen estate to Job's guilt, since prosperity spared and adversity sent alike wait upon a judgment not yet come. The wicked man's escape, rightly read, is not a verdict of innocence but a stay of execution.
31:
So untouchable is the prospering wicked man that none dares call him to account: "who shall declare his way to his face? and who shall repay him what he hath done?" The reformed John Gill notes that some, with Jarchi and Aben Ezra, refer the words to God, that none may presume to charge his providence with injustice for sparing the wicked now; but Gill himself refers them to the wicked man, so great in wealth and honour as to be above reproof: his way is a wicked course of life, and he ought to be told the evil of it to his face by his kindred and acquaintance, yet none dares.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh both constructions and decide against the reference to God. The common reading takes the verse as a reflection on the exemption of the evil-doer, that God's mode of action is exalted above all human scrutiny; but the clause "who will recompense it to him," used of a man toward God, yields no fitting sense, and so with most expositors the words must be understood of the evil-doer: so powerful is the wicked that no one can oppose his pernicious doings and call him to account, much less venture to repay him according to his desert when once he has carried his purpose through. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says it in a line: his power and splendour are so great that scarce any man dares reprove him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the impunity into an argument for a judgment to come: while the wicked is in power, who shall dare tell him to his face what his true character is, or repay him the evil he has done? and since such a man cannot have his punishment in this life, he must have it in another, for which the day of wrath, the day of judgment, is prepared. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the same fact the ruinous fruit of prosperity: it sets the sinner, in his own conceit, above reproof, so that none dares declare his way to his face, and he sins securely, knowing neither shame nor fear; those are marked for destruction who are thus let alone in sin, as at Hosea 4:17. The witnesses do not divide, save on whose face is meant; they agree that the wicked man's greatness has lifted him beyond all earthly rebuke and requital, and that this very unaccountableness, so far from proving him blessed, is the surest sign that his reckoning is only deferred to a bar he cannot overawe.
32:
Even in death the great sinner is attended with honour, for "yet shall he be brought to the grave, and shall remain in the tomb." The reformed John Gill is careful that this is no come-down: Job is still describing the grand figure the wicked man makes, even at his death as in his life. He is not merely brought to the grave as all men are, but brought in great funeral pomp and state, buried in the choicest of his ancestors' sepulchres, given an honourable interment, not cast into a ditch nor buried with the burial of an ass; and there he shall remain quiet and undisturbed, when others have had their very bones taken out of the grave.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the plain sense, that he dies like other men and the corruption of the grave preys upon him, but then reports a striking gloss from Arabic poetry: the words may be rendered "he shall watch upon the high-raised heap," for the pagan Arabs held that on a man's death a bird issued from the brain and haunted the sepulchre with a lamentable scream, a notion he finds alluded to here. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the very word rendered "tomb," which elsewhere, at Job 5:26, means a shock of corn and is nowhere else found in the sense of a tomb; the verse may therefore mean "he shall be borne to the grave, and men shall watch over his sheaves," that is, his possessions, or "borne to the grave with as much deference as when he used to watch over his sheaves" to guard them from robbery. So a real difference stands over the second clause, whether it speaks of a watch kept over the tomb or over the dead man's hoarded wealth.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, keep to the funeral sense and render "he is brought to the grave, and over the tomb he still keepeth watch," taking the plural of "tombs" as an amplifying form for a splendid sepulchre, the same word "brought" that is used of an honourable conveyance elsewhere in the book. The witnesses do not divide over the main thing. They agree that Job caps his portrait of the wicked man's charmed life with a stately death: the oppressor who escaped all reproof escapes even the disgrace of the grave, borne to a fine tomb with every honour, and left to rest there in peace; and that this pomp of burial, so far from any mark of wrath, is the last and most galling refutation of the friends, who had promised the wicked a ruin visible to all.
33:
"The clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him," and the very earth of his grave lies light on the great sinner. The reformed John Gill reads the sweetness as repose: interred in some well-chosen vale beneath the hills, the dead wicked man lies in the utmost ease and quiet, feeling no pain of body and no uneasiness of mind over what befalls his posterity after him. The clods lie sweet upon him because nothing now can reach him, neither pain in the body nor grief for the house he has left. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sees in the phrase an allusion to a princely burial, a well-watered valley chosen for the tomb where a perpetual spring might keep the turf green, emblem of a life to come and a veil over the disgrace of the rotting body.

The closing clause draws the witnesses to the long procession of the dead. Clarke hears in "every man shall draw after him" two things at once: death the common lot of all, millions gone before and all men to follow, and the pomp of a great funeral, multitudes preceding and multitudes following the corpse. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it wholly of honour: death is robbed of its repulsiveness, seeing that all are glad to join his funeral procession, drawn after him in endless train while before him they went without number. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, render the line the same, every man drawing after him as innumerable went before, and carry it straight into the retort of the final verse.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes the valley as the low, deep grave, where the wicked man shall sweetly rest, and reads the drawing after him of all mankind who live after him and must die as he did; he is figuratively said to draw them because they follow, as if by his example. In this at least, Wesley notes, the great sinner fares no worse than all men, going the common way of the earth. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job ends his portrait where the friends least expected, at a grave made sweet and a funeral thronged, the ungodly man carried to his rest with the honours of a multitude and the whole race falling into line behind him; and that this serene and crowded ending, no bands in his death and no terror at his tomb, is the finished answer to every comforter who read God's wrath in a man's outward fall. The sweet grave and the thronged funeral are Job's last and quietest witnesses against the doctrine of a visible retribution.
34:
"How then comfort ye me in vain, seeing in your answers there remaineth falsehood?" With this Job draws the whole chapter to its verdict, and the witnesses read it as the collapse of the comforters' scheme. The reformed John Gill states the conclusion: his friends had come to comfort him, but miserable comforters were they all, for what they administered was in vain and to no purpose, resting as it did on the maxim that his afflictions proved him a bad man and that reformation would restore his prosperity; and that maxim the instances just rehearsed had overthrown, since the wicked enjoy prosperity and good men often bear a great share of adversity. The comfort had a false foundation, and a house built on it could not stand; where the premise fails, Gill says, the consolation drawn from it fails with it.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the first clause to the friends' vain attempt to make Job retract, and then stands back to survey the chapter. He cannot retract anything he has said, having proved by fact and testimony that their positions are false, and their offered comfort is as hollow as their doctrine. Clarke calls the chapter Job's triumph over the insinuated calumnies and specious doctrines of his opponents: the irritability of his earlier temper no longer appears, for since he saw his Redeemer and grasped the hope of an eternal inheritance he murmurs no more, but reasons coolly and conclusively, his mind serene, his hope steady, his faith strong, standing to the stroke like a beaten anvil. The chapter, on Clarke's reading, marks the turn in Job from passion to composure, a man now master of himself because he has become master of his hope.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the last word: what remains in their answers is not merely worthless but "transgression," all that is left of them being harmful and wrong, a positive fault and not a bare mistake. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the plain sense together: why then do you seek to comfort me with vain hopes of recovered prosperity, when your grounds are false, and experience shows that good men are often in great tribulation while the vilest of men prosper? The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the chapter ends by pronouncing the friends' comfort empty at its root: built on a false rule of retribution, their consolation could yield nothing but falsehood, and where there is no truth there is no comfort; Job has met their doctrine with the stubborn facts of the world and left it, in Ellicott's word, not merely useless but wrong. The comforters are dismissed with their own medicine named at last for what it is.
